title: Don't Just Prepare Them to Use It. Prepare Them to Change It.
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek argues that the dominant AI-in-schools conversation, focused on responsible use, prompt literacy, and acceptable-use policies, is aimed at an insufficient target because it prepares students to be highly competent users of tools they have no ability to understand or reshape. He draws a direct parallel to social media digital-citizenship education, which produced a generation of sophisticated platform users with zero technical ability to contest or change how recommendation algorithms actually worked, and argues AI education is on the identical path with higher stakes. Using the metaphor of passengers versus pilots, he argues that teaching only use produces 'highly capable passengers' who know the safety procedures but have no say in where the plane goes. His concrete proposal is to teach real, demystified technical content, how training data and loss functions shape model behavior, and give students hands-on practice modifying small models, reframing AI literacy as a strand of civic education rather than digital citizenship, since these systems increasingly make decisions once made by humans accountable to democratic processes.
points: Argues that AI-in-schools efforts focused on responsible use, prompt literacy, and acceptable-use policy are insufficient because they train competent users of tools students have no technical ability to understand or reshape.
Draws a direct historical parallel to social-media digital citizenship education, which produced sophisticated platform users with zero ability to contest or change harmful recommendation algorithms.
Uses a passengers-versus-pilots metaphor: teaching only use produces 'highly capable passengers' who know safety procedures but have no say in where the system takes them.

Proposes concrete technical content -- demystified understanding of training data, loss functions, and hands-on practice modifying small models -- reframed as civic education rather than digital citizenship, since AI increasingly makes decisions once made by democratically accountable humans.
quotes: We are preparing an entire generation of students to be highly competent users of tools that other people built, for purposes other people decided, with values other people encoded, and we are calling that preparation for the future.
None of it gave a single student the ability to say, this recommendation algorithm is optimizing for engagement in a way that is harmful, and here is how I would build it differently.
If we only teach students to use AI tools well, we are training a generation of highly capable passengers.
They still don't know how to fly the plane, and more importantly, they have no say in where it goes.

It would mean giving students actual practice modifying, not just prompting, small models, seeing firsthand what happens when you change a training objective or a dataset, so the black box becomes at least partially a glass box.

But if we only ever prepare kids to be sophisticated passengers, we should not be surprised, twenty years from now, when they have exactly as much say over where AI takes society as this generation had over where social media took us.
